The postoperative wound has become purulent. From the pus we isolate a pure culture, identify the species by coagulase and test for MRSA.
Pain and swelling of the surgical suture, rising temperature, thick yellow discharge from the suture.
A planned hernioplasty was performed 6 days ago. The temperature has been elevated since day 4. Received cefazolin for prophylaxis.
The area around the suture is red, warm and tender on palpation; thick, yellowish, odorless pus comes from the edge of the suture. Temperature ⟦0⟧ °C.

Isolate a **pure culture** from the pus and identify the pathogen.
Perform the **key test** that distinguishes staphylococci from one another.
Set up an **antibiogram** and assess resistance to methicillin (MRSA).

__Staphylococcus aureus__ is a Gram-positive, spherical coccus arranged in **grape-like clusters**. It is non-motile, does not form spores and is a facultative anaerobe. The name comes from its golden-yellow pigment (Lat. __aureus__ — golden).

**Virulence factors:** plasma coagulase (forms a fibrin coat and protects against phagocytosis), lecithinase, hyaluronidase, DNase, protein A (binds the Fc part of IgG), hemolysins, leukocidin, exfoliative toxin, TSST-1, enterotoxins.
**Clinical forms:** purulent wound infection, abscess, furuncle, mastitis, osteomyelitis, pneumonia, endocarditis, sepsis; with enterotoxin — food poisoning.
**MRSA** is a strain resistant to methicillin (and therefore to all beta-lactams); the resistance arises from the altered PBP2a protein encoded by the __mecA__ gene.
Staphylococci: grape-like clusters in a smear stained by the Gram method.

Bacteriological diagnosis is a multi-step process: **specimen collection → bacterioscopy → isolation streaking on solid medium → study of colonies → pure culture → biochemical identification → antibiogram**.

**The Gram method** is based on the structure of the cell wall: thick peptidoglycan is dehydrated by alcohol and retains the gentian violet–iodine complex (Gram+ — purple); cells with thin peptidoglycan lose this complex and are stained red by fuchsin (Gram− — red).
**Blood agar** is an enriched medium: it allows the type of hemolysis to be assessed. __S. aureus__ gives complete (beta) hemolysis.
**Egg-yolk salt agar** is a selective medium: 7.5–10 % NaCl inhibits other microbes while staphylococci grow; lecithinase produces a cloudy (opalescent) zone around the colony.
**Plasma coagulase** is the key test for species identification: __S. aureus__ (+), __S. epidermidis__ and __S. saprophyticus__ (−).
**Disk diffusion method (Kirby–Bauer)**: the antibiotic diffuses from the disk into the agar; the diameter of the zone of inhibited growth is converted to S / I / R by the standard table.

A coagulase-positive, mannitol-positive, golden-pigmented, beta-hemolytic Gram-positive coccus is __S. aureus__. __S. epidermidis__ is coagulase-negative, __S. pyogenes__ is catalase-negative.

The disk diffusion method is **unreliable** for vancomycin: the zone diameter does not reflect resistance. That is why vancomycin is assessed only by **MIC**.
Why is the result of the cefoxitin disk especially important?
**It detects methicillin resistance linked to the __mecA__ gene, and the result extends to all beta-lactams**

Cefoxitin is the best inducer and indicator of __mecA__ / PBP2a. If cefoxitin is R, the strain is considered MRSA and penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems are all reported as ineffective, even if the in vitro zone comes out large.
Which two groups does the catalase test separate?
Both groups are Gram-positive cocci, but staphylococci have the enzyme catalase. That is why catalase is the first step in the identification of cocci.
What role does the enzyme plasma coagulase play in pathogenicity?
**Forms a fibrin coat around the microbe and protects it from phagocytosis**
Coagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin; the resulting film hides the bacterium from phagocytes and walls off the focus, leading to abscess formation.
How does the antibiogram result change if the suspension is prepared thicker than 0.5 McFarland?
**The zones get smaller and a susceptible strain looks resistant**
If many cells are seeded, the amount of antibiotic that has diffused is not enough to stop growth — the zone comes out small. In a thin suspension, on the contrary, false susceptibility is obtained.

This is also why the cefazolin given to the patient before the operation did not work.

Opening, washing and draining the wound — an antibiotic alone is not enough in a purulent focus. Systemic treatment: **vancomycin** or **linezolid**; according to the antibiogram, co-trimoxazole and clindamycin are also susceptible. The vancomycin dose is adjusted to the MIC and renal function.

__Streptococcus pyogenes__ (group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, GABHS) is a Gram-positive, spherical coccus arranged **in chains**. It is catalase-negative, a facultative anaerobe and fastidious (grows on blood agar).

**Virulence factors:** M protein (the main virulence factor, resistance to phagocytosis), streptolysin O and S (hemolysins), hyaluronidase, streptokinase (fibrinolysin), DNase, erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin — the cause of the scarlet fever rash.
**Acute diseases:** tonsillitis (tonsillopharyngitis), scarlet fever, erysipelas, impetigo, necrotizing fasciitis, sepsis.

**Late (immune) complications:** acute rheumatic fever and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. They arise not from the microbe itself but from the **similarity between M protein and heart/kidney tissue antigens** (molecular mimicry).
Streptococci: chain-like arrangement in a smear stained by the Gram method.
**Blood agar** — beta-hemolysis (a completely cleared zone around the colony) is typical of group A streptococci; alpha-hemolysis (green zone) of pneumococci and oral streptococci.
The **catalase test** distinguishes from staphylococci: streptococci are **catalase-negative**.
**Bacitracin disk (0.04 U)** — group A streptococci are **susceptible** to bacitracin, other groups are usually resistant. This is a simple and cheap preliminary grouping method.
**Latex agglutination** — a more accurate method that directly detects the group polysaccharide antigen (A, B, C, G by Lancefield).
**ASO** (antistreptolysin O) — the titer of antibodies against streptolysin O; shows a **past** infection and the risk of an immune complication, and is not for acute diagnosis.

Beta-hemolysis is the **complete** breakdown of erythrocytes under the action of streptolysins: a clear, transparent halo around the colony. Alpha-hemolysis gives a **green** zone through partial breakdown and oxidation of hemoglobin.

Features: Gram+ coccus in chains, beta-hemolysis, catalase −, bacitracin susceptible, latex group A. Species:

Beta-hemolysis + bacitracin susceptibility + group A latex — the classic set for __S. pyogenes__. The pneumococcus is alpha-hemolytic and optochin-susceptible, while the enterococcus is bacitracin-resistant.

**Penicillin resistance has still not been reported** in __S. pyogenes__ — so penicillin remains the drug of choice. Resistance to macrolides does occur, and in this patient erythromycin came out resistant.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a **DNA virus** of the family __Hepadnaviridae__. The complete particle is the **Dane particle**: inside, double-stranded DNA and its own DNA polymerase (with reverse transcriptase activity), outside, an envelope with surface antigen.
**HBsAg** (surface antigen, the “Australia antigen”) is the envelope protein; its presence in the blood is a sign of **active infection**. If it persists for more than 6 months — chronic infection.
**HBcAg** (core antigen) is not found free in the blood (it is in the hepatocyte nucleus); **anti-HBc** antibodies against it are detected.
**HBeAg** is the soluble part of the core antigen; it indicates that **the virus is actively replicating and the risk of transmission is high**.
**Routes of transmission:** parenteral (medical procedures, injections, tattoos), sexual, perinatal (mother to child). HBV is stable in the environment and is much more infectious than HIV.
**Outcome:** acute hepatitis → recovery or chronicity → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma. In adults chronicity is ~5 %, in newborns up to **90 %**.

**Antibodies** (anti-HBs, anti-HBc, anti-HBe) show the body's response.

**The “window period”:** the interval when HBsAg has disappeared and anti-HBs has not yet appeared — in this period the **only positive marker is anti-HBc IgM**. So it must be in the panel.

Principle of the method: a two-stage examination

**Stage 1 — screening (ELISA):** tuned for high **sensitivity**, that is, aimed at not missing a sick person. So false-positive results are possible (pregnancy, autoimmune diseases, recent vaccination).

**Stage 2 — confirmatory (immunoblot):** has high **specificity**. Viral proteins are separated by electrophoresis according to molecular weight and transferred to a membrane; antibodies in the patient's serum bind to the matching band.

**Mandatory conditions of testing:** the patient's **voluntary consent**, counseling before and after the test, and **confidentiality** of the result.

**RT-PCR (reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction):** the viral RNA is first converted into DNA by **reverse transcriptase**, then doubles with each cycle. The signal, via a fluorescent probe, is followed in real time.

The cause of malaria is a protozoan of the genus __Plasmodium__. There are four main species in humans: __P. falciparum__ (tropical malaria, the most dangerous), __P. vivax__, __P. ovale__ and __P. malariae__. The vector is **a female mosquito of the genus __Anopheles__**.

**Life cycle:** when the mosquito bites, sporozoites enter the blood → multiply in the liver (**tissue cycle**) → merozoites enter the blood and invade erythrocytes (**erythrocytic cycle**) → ring form, trophozoite, schizont → the erythrocyte ruptures and new merozoites are released.
**The fever attack** coincides with the simultaneous rupture of erythrocytes — so the attacks are periodic.

__P. falciparum__ is **dangerous** because: it infects erythrocytes of any age (parasitemia becomes very high), infected erythrocytes adhere to the capillary endothelium (sequestration) and lead to organ ischemia — **cerebral malaria**, acute kidney failure, severe anemia.
__P. vivax__ and __P. ovale__ persist in the liver as **hypnozoites** and cause a **relapse** months later — so they need additional treatment (primaquine).

When should the blood be taken?
During a fever attack or just before it, from a fingertip
During an attack the number of parasites in the blood is at its highest.
One day after the temperature falls
parasitemia falls and the parasite becomes harder to find
After an antimalarial drug has been started
treatment sharply reduces the number of parasites — false-negative result
the clot traps the parasites; for a smear anticoagulant must be added or fresh capillary blood is needed
What is done if the first test is negative?
**It is repeated at 12–24 hour intervals, 3 times in all**
Only a rapid test is done
Parasitemia fluctuates in waves and may be low between attacks. A single negative result does not exclude malaria.
A rapid immunochromatographic test (RDT) may be set up at the same time, but microscopy remains the gold standard.
What do you see in the thin smear?
**Small, delicate ring forms inside erythrocytes; several in some erythrocytes**
The ring form (a delicate ring + a red-violet nuclear dot) is the erythrocytic stage of the malaria parasite. Several rings in one erythrocyte are typical of __P. falciparum__.
Crescent-shaped (banana-shaped) gametocytes were also seen in the smear. Which species is this typical of?
A crescent-shaped gametocyte is a sign of **__P. falciparum__ only**. In the other species the gametocytes are round. This difference completely changes treatment tactics.
Of 1000 erythrocytes counted, ⟦0⟧ are infected. Calculate the parasitemia.
Parasitemia = infected erythrocytes / total erythrocytes × 100 = ⟦0⟧ / 1000 × 100 = **⟦1⟧ %**. This figure assesses severity: a parasitemia above 5 % is one of the criteria of severe malaria.
We assess the severity criteria: in malaria the decision determines the place of treatment (outpatient or intensive care).
What is the significance of thrombocytopenia in malaria?
It is not a sign of complication
**It is very common in malaria and is an additional reason to think of malaria in a febrile patient**
Thrombocytopenia is one of the most consistent laboratory signs of malaria. In a patient returning from a tropical country, febrile and with a low platelet count, the probability of malaria is high.
**Impaired consciousness, parasitemia > 5 %, severe anemia, kidney failure, hypoglycemia, acidosis**
The criteria of severe malaria determine the place and route of treatment: if present, the patient is admitted to intensive care and given intravenous artesunate.

Parasitemia ⟦0⟧ % — close to the 5 % threshold; consciousness is clear, kidney function and glucose are normal. So for now it is assessed as **uncomplicated** tropical malaria, but parasitemia is followed over time.
Why are two preparations (thick drop and thin smear) prepared?
**They have different purposes: the thick drop is for finding the parasite (high sensitivity), the thin smear for identifying the species and calculating the parasitemia**
They are identical, as a backup

In the thick drop the erythrocytes are hemolyzed — a lot of blood is examined, but the cell structure is lost. In the thin smear the erythrocytes are preserved — the species is identified. The two complement each other.
Why is __P. falciparum__ considered the most dangerous species?
**It infects erythrocytes of any age (high parasitemia) and infected erythrocytes adhere to the capillary endothelium, leading to organ ischemia — cerebral malaria**
Drugs do not act on it
Because of sequestration, infected erythrocytes block small vessels. That is why the brain, kidneys and lungs are damaged; the disease can become life-threatening within a few days.
Why is an additional drug (primaquine) given in __P. vivax__ malaria?
**To eliminate the hypnozoites in the liver — without it a relapse occurs months later**
Drugs that act on the forms in the blood do not act on the dormant hypnozoites in the liver. __P. falciparum__ has no hypnozoites, so it does not relapse.
If the first thick drop is negative, which decision is correct?
**Repeat the test 3 times at 12–24 hour intervals**
Rely only on the rapid test
Parasitemia falls between attacks. If clinical suspicion persists, a repeat test is essential; a rapid test is set up at the same time.
What is the most important preventive measure for travelers?
**Protection from mosquito bites and chemoprophylaxis matched to the region**

A widely used vaccine against malaria is still limited. The main measures are mosquito protection (nets, repellent, covering clothing) and chemoprophylaxis started before the trip. This patient took no chemoprophylaxis.
**Tropical malaria (__Plasmodium falciparum__)**, parasitemia ⟦0⟧ %; uncomplicated for now.

Periodic fever attacks that began 2 weeks after returning from Africa, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin ⟦0⟧ g/L, indirect bilirubin raised) and thrombocytopenia (⟦1⟧ × 10⁹/L) — a picture typical of malaria. A parasite was found in the thick drop; in the thin smear small ring-form trophozoites, several in one erythrocyte, and **crescent-shaped gametocytes** — __P. falciparum__. Consciousness is clear, and kidney function and glucose are normal — no criteria of severe malaria so far.

In __P. falciparum__ malaria **artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)** is the treatment of choice. If signs of severe malaria appear — intravenous **artesunate** and intensive care. Parasitemia and hemoglobin are followed over time; hypoglycemia, anemia and fluid balance are monitored. Since __P. falciparum__ has no hypnozoites, a primaquine course (against relapse) is **not needed**.

For those traveling to an endemic area: **chemoprophylaxis** started before the trip, insecticide-treated mosquito nets, repellents, covering clothing in the evening. If fever appears after returning — seek care at once and tell the doctor about the trip. In the area: eliminate water bodies where mosquitoes breed.
Interpreting an immunogram: recurrent bacterial infections
A child with recurrent pneumonia and otitis. We read the immunogram step by step and determine which link of immunity is deficient.
Recurrent purulent infections: over the last two years several episodes of pneumonia and middle ear inflammation, chronic sinusitis.

Has been treated in hospital ⟦0⟧ times for pneumonia and ⟦1⟧ times for purulent otitis. Each time responded well to antibiotics, but the infections recur. Was healthy during the first 6 months. His maternal uncle had a similar illness in childhood.
Physical development lags behind his age. **The tonsils and cervical lymph nodes are very small or not palpable.** No rales in the lungs at present.
On the complete blood count the leukocytes are normal and the lymphocyte count is within the normal range. HIV negative.
Immunogram — blood was drawn to assess the main links of immunity.
Assess **the three links** of the immunogram in turn.
Determine in which link the defect lies and explain it logically.
Compare with the signs in the history and decide the conclusion and the direction of treatment.

An immunogram is a set of tests that assess the main links of the immune system **at the same time**. It gives not a single indicator but **a picture**: it shows which link is not working and so sets the direction of diagnosis.
**Cellular link:** CD3⁺ (total T lymphocytes), CD4⁺ (helper), CD8⁺ (cytotoxic), CD16⁺/CD56⁺ (NK cells). Determined by flow cytometry.
**Humoral link:** CD19⁺ (B lymphocytes) and immunoglobulins — **IgG, IgA, IgM** (IgG is the main defense, IgA on mucosal surfaces, IgM in the first response).
**Phagocytic link:** the neutrophil count, phagocytic activity, the NBT test (oxygen-dependent bactericidal activity).
**Complement system:** C3, C4, total hemolytic activity (CH50).
Which infections occur when each link is impaired?
**Recurrent purulent** infections caused by encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, __H. influenzae__): pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis
Viruses, fungi, intracellular pathogens (tuberculosis, Pneumocystis, candidiasis)
Abscesses of the skin and internal organs, staphylococcal and fungal infections
Separating the lymphocytes on a gradient — preparation for flow cytometry.

A newborn receives **IgG** from the mother through the placenta; it disappears at 3–6 months. So humoral deficiency often shows itself **after 6 months** — in this patient too the first 6 months passed healthily.
In children the normal range of immunoglobulins is **age-dependent** — the result is always compared with the age-appropriate range.
**Small lymphoid tissue** (tonsils, lymph nodes not palpable) may be a clinical sign of a lack of B cells, because the follicles of the lymph nodes are made up precisely of B cells.

An immunogram is **never interpreted in isolation**: it is assessed together with the age, the clinical picture and the type of infections. Otherwise even a value at the lower limit of normal may be wrongly judged as “disease”.
Recurrent **purulent** infections (pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis) first make one think of which link being impaired?
The late components of the complement system

The basis of defense against encapsulated bacteria is **opsonizing antibodies**. If they are lacking, recurrent purulent infections caused by pneumococcus and __H. influenzae__ appear. In T-cell deficiency, viral and fungal infections would predominate.
The type of infections shows which link must be examined.
Taking blood and preparing the sample
CD19 (B cells) and IgG, IgA, IgM.
Neutrophils, phagocytic activity, the NBT test.
Comparing the results with the age norms
In children the normal range depends on age.
The picture is compared with the clinical findings.
Replacement therapy and protection from infections.
Choose the condition for taking the sample for an immunogram.
Blood taken outside an acute infection, in the morning, on an empty stomach
Acute infection and stress temporarily change the values — the result does not reflect the patient's true state.
during acute inflammation the values change temporarily and the conclusion will be wrong
In the middle of a glucocorticoid course
hormones sharply reduce the lymphocyte count — a false picture of deficiency
The day after an immunoglobulin infusion
the administered IgG makes the level falsely normal
The sampling condition determines the reliability of the immunogram result — this is the most overlooked part of the test.
Separating the lymphocytes and preparing for flow cytometry.
We read the immunogram **link by link in turn**: first the cellular, then the humoral, and last the phagocytic link. This order shows the site of the defect precisely.
How is the cellular link (CD3, CD4, CD8, NK) assessed?
**All values are within the age norm — the cellular link is preserved**
T cells and NK cells are normal. So defense against viruses, fungi and intracellular pathogens is working — this fits the type of infections in this patient too.
What do you see in the humoral link?
**CD19⁺ B lymphocytes are almost absent (0.4 %) and all three immunoglobulins are sharply reduced**
This is the main finding: the absence of B cells and a fall in **all** immunoglobulin classes. If only IgA were reduced, this would be selective IgA deficiency.
How are the phagocytic link and complement?
**Normal — phagocytic activity, the NBT test and C3 are unchanged**
These links are preserved. So the defect is **only in the humoral link** — the picture is clear and points in one direction.
No B cells, all immunoglobulins low, T cells normal, a boy, the illness began after 6 months, an uncle had a similar condition. What is the most likely conclusion?

The set of signs is typical: **a boy** (X-linked), illness **after 6 months** (once maternal IgG has run out), **no B cells**, all immunoglobulins low, T cells normal, small lymphoid tissue and a similar illness **on the maternal side**. In SCID the T cells would also be absent and the illness would begin much earlier and be more severe.
tonsils and lymph nodes very small
The picture is clear: **only the humoral link** is impaired — B cells are almost absent and all three immunoglobulins are low, while the cellular and phagocytic links and complement are preserved.
Why did the illness in this child begin precisely after 6 months?
**Until then the IgG received from the mother through the placenta protected him; when it ran out, the absence of his own antibodies showed itself**
Maternal IgG disappears at 3–6 months. So humoral deficiencies almost always show clinically after this age — an important diagnostic clue in the history.
Why are **encapsulated** bacteria (pneumococcus, __H. influenzae__) in particular dangerous in this patient?
**The capsule resists phagocytosis; overcoming it needs opsonization with antibodies, and the antibodies are absent**
Antibodies “tag” the bacterium and make it recognizable to phagocytes. Without them an encapsulated bacterium hides from the phagocytes — so recurrent pneumonia, otitis and sinusitis appear.
What does the very small size of the tonsils and lymph nodes show?
**The follicles of the lymph nodes are made up of B cells; without B cells, lymphoid tissue does not develop**
This is a sign visible on an ordinary examination but very valuable: it lets one predict the immunogram result in advance.
Can **live** vaccines be given to such a patient?
**Caution is needed: live vaccines can be dangerous in immunodeficiency, and this question is decided with a specialist**
Vaccination is not needed at all

In immunodeficiency live vaccines can cause vaccine-associated disease. In addition, in a patient who cannot form antibodies the benefit of a vaccine is limited — protection is provided mainly by replacement immunoglobulin.
What is the most important rule in interpreting an immunogram?
Look only at the lowest value
**Assess the result link by link, together with the age norms and the clinical picture**

A single value can be misleading. The picture — which link is impaired and which infections this fits — gives the diagnosis. In this patient the type of infections and the immunogram match completely.
**Primary immunodeficiency — an impaired humoral link; X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's disease) is suspected.**

Recurrent purulent infections (⟦0⟧ episodes of pneumonia, ⟦1⟧ of otitis, chronic sinusitis) point to impaired defense against encapsulated bacteria. On the immunogram CD19⁺ B lymphocytes are almost absent (0.4 %), IgG ⟦2⟧ g/L, IgA 0.06 g/L and IgM 0.11 g/L — all classes sharply low. The cellular link (CD3, CD4, CD8, NK), phagocytosis and complement are normal. Onset of the illness after 6 months, male sex, small lymphoid tissue and a family history on the maternal side support the diagnosis. For final confirmation a **genetic test (the __BTK__ gene)** is required.

**Regular immunoglobulin replacement therapy** (intravenous or subcutaneous, at regular intervals) is the main treatment; it keeps the IgG level within the protective range. Early and adequate antibiotics for infections; in some cases prophylactic antibiotics. **Live vaccines are limited according to the specialist's decision.** Immunologist follow-up, regular monitoring of the lungs (risk of chronic bronchiectasis).

Genetic counseling for the family (X-linked inheritance: the mother may be a carrier); protection from infections and early treatment of them; seasonal vaccination of those around (this indirectly protects the patient); placing the child under follow-up and monitoring growth and development.
